addressed_problems.content: Despite empirical success in finding tiny trainable subnetworks (winning tickets) for worst-case VCG redistribution mechanism design via repeated pruning from a fixed initial large network, there is no theoretical guarantee that this procedure will converge to a winning ticket within any computable number of draws. The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis only suggests existence but does not provide conditions or bounds for this specific mechanism design task, where the subnetwork is evaluated via MIP-based worst-case training. Proving sufficient conditions on the initial network size, architecture, or training process that ensure a winning ticket must exist, or establishing a finite bound on the expected number of draws needed to encounter one, remains an open theoretical problem.

The mixed integer programming (MIP) formulation used for exact worst-case certification of VCG redistribution mechanisms requires one binary variable for every hidden node of the RELU network and for every agent, making the approach computationally intractable for larger numbers of agents or larger subnetworks. In practice, with 128 GB memory, the method reaches its scalability limit around n=20 even when using very small tickets (e.g., 6 nodes). Developing certified worst-case search methods that scale to larger n or to larger subnetworks—for example via tighter continuous relaxations, symmetry exploitation, or alternative exact-certification encodings that avoid the per-node-per-agent binary variable blow-up—is an open research direction.

For the public project problem with n=3,4,5 agents, the paper identifies VCG redistribution mechanisms whose worst-case allocative efficiency ratios match the conjectured theoretical upper bounds to within a small numerical gap (less than 0.0001). However, for n≥6, the true optimal worst-case allocative efficiency ratio remains unknown, and it is unresolved whether the theoretical upper bounds proposed in [25] are tight. Although the paper derives significantly improved mechanisms for up to 20 agents that surpass a long list of manual results, these are not proven optimal, and the question of whether the bounds can be achieved for all n≥6 remains open.

All near-optimal VCG redistribution mechanisms discovered in this paper are represented as RELU neural networks with floating-point weights obtained through stochastic gradient descent and MIP-based training. Floating-point numerical error prevents formal exact-symbolic proofs of optimality; the claimed near-optimal worst-case allocative efficiency ratios are only guaranteed up to the precision of the floating-point computation (e.g., gaps less than 0.0001). Producing exact rational or symbolic descriptions of the optimal Groves term h—analogous to the closed-form rational mechanisms found for n=3—and providing analytical proofs of optimality (for n=4,5 and potentially beyond) remains an open task.

The paper presents multiple distinct optimal VCG redistribution mechanisms for n=3 agents, and empirical evidence suggests that for n≥4 there may also exist many distinct optimal mechanisms (i.e., different Groves terms h that achieve the same worst-case allocative efficiency ratio). However, the combinatorial or geometric structure of the set of optimal h functions is not understood. Characterizing the multiplicity of optimal mechanisms for larger n—for example, whether the optimal h is unique up to trivial symmetries, or whether there is a continuous family of optimal solutions—and deriving the underlying structural properties of the optimal Groves terms remains an open theoretical problem.

The work studies the classical public project mechanism-design setting in which $n$ agents decide whether to build a non-excludable binary public project that costs 1, each agent $i$ having a privately known value $\theta_i\in[0,1]$, and efficient allocation is to build iff $\sum_i\theta_i\ge 1$. By Holmström's characterization any strategy-proof and efficient mechanism must be a Groves mechanism; restricting attention to VCG redistribution mechanisms reduces the design task to choosing a Groves term $h(\theta_{-i})$ (a function of the other agents' reports) subject to the non-deficit constraint. The objective is to maximize the worst-case allocative efficiency ratio $\alpha$, requiring for every type profile $\vec\theta$ that $(n-1)s(\vec\theta)\le\sum_i h(\theta_{-i})\le (n-\alpha)s(\vec\theta)$ where $s(\vec\theta)=\max\{\sum_i\theta_i,1\}$. Prior work established theoretical upper bounds on the achievable worst-case $\alpha$ and solved the exact optimal mechanism only in a handful of low-dimensional cases (notably $n=3$), while for $n\ge 4$ whether the bounds are tight remained unresolved. Existing automated or neural-network based approaches typically relied on Monte Carlo worst-case estimation (which can dramatically overestimate worst-case performance) or manual/partial automated designs; moreover, exact certification of worst-case violations for RELU-based networks via mixed-integer programming (MIP) requires one binary variable per network node per agent and thus becomes computationally infeasible for anything but tiny networks. Consequently, two interlocking technical gaps prevented progress: (i) the need for an exact, certifiable worst-case evaluation method that can be integrated into training to produce mechanisms with guaranteed worst-case performance, and (ii) the need for a principled way to obtain tiny trainable RELU subnetworks (so that exact MIP-based certification is computationally tractable) rather than relying on repeated random reinitializations or Monte Carlo. These gaps prevented discovery of optimal or near-optimal worst-case VCG redistribution mechanisms for $n\ge 4$, limited mechanistic understanding of the structure of optimal $h$ functions for larger $n$, and obstructed reliable scaling of exact worst-case design techniques beyond very small $n$.

nodes.content: In the public project setting researchers must choose function classes to represent candidate Groves terms $h(\theta_{-i})$ when attempting automated worst-case design. If optimal $h$ functions were necessarily discontinuous, RELU-MLPs (or any continuous approximator) might be inadequate; relying on such approximators could then fundamentally preclude reaching the optimal worst-case $\alpha$. Prior work therefore left open whether restricting attention to continuous $h$ (and hence to RELU-MLP parametrizations) could lose worst-case optimality. The absence of a formal approximation guarantee made it unclear whether a neural-network-based search could, even in principle, approach the true optimal $\alpha$.

Effective worst-case mechanism design requires exact knowledge of the true worst-case constraint violations for a candidate Groves term $h$. Prior neural-network approaches that estimated worst-case behavior by Monte Carlo sampling produced optimistic (inflated) assessments and could not provide certification that a candidate $h$ met non-deficit or worst-case performance guarantees. A method that, for a fixed RELU-MLP $h$, computes the true global maximizers of the violation objectives and returns both the numerical violation amounts and the exact worst-case profiles is therefore necessary. However, encoding RELU networks and the non-deficit constraint exactly requires binary activation variables that scale with the product of agents and network nodes, creating severe computational bottlenecks that force the use of tiny networks unless a principled means of obtaining tiny trainable subnetworks is available.

Even with exact MIP certification for a fixed $h$, a practical mechanism-design procedure must search the space of $h$ functions efficiently. Blind stochastic optimization can be trapped in local minima and is impractical when every evaluation step may require expensive MIP certification. Prior training loops either ignored exact certification or performed it only as an offline audit; neither approach produces models trained specifically to minimize worst-case certified violations. There is thus a need for a training protocol that (a) focuses training on the true worst-case profiles produced by exact certification, (b) limits the number of expensive certification calls to tractable amounts, and (c) employs curriculum-like goal adjustment so the optimizer does not attempt infeasible targets too early. Without such a protocol it is infeasible to obtain guarantees or to steadily improve provable worst-case $\alpha$ in practice.

The MIP exact-certification method requires tiny networks (one binary per node per agent) to be computationally feasible, yet directly training tiny networks from random initializations almost always fails because trainability depends strongly on initialization—many tiny initializations lead to poor local optima. Randomly reinitializing tiny networks a practical number of times does not reliably produce a trainable initialization. The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis suggests large networks contain sparse, trainable subnetworks, but a procedure is needed to systematically find such subnetworks while avoiding repeated selection of poor tickets and while enabling exact MIP-based evaluation on each candidate ticket. Prior approaches neither exploited pruning from a fixed initial large network nor incorporated worst-case profiles from failed tickets to steer future draws; without those mechanisms, one cannot both (i) discover tiny subnetworks that yield good worst-case certified performance and (ii) make repeated draws computationally effective.

For $n\ge 4$ prior research had been unable to produce explicit mechanisms matching the theoretical upper bounds; for $n=3$ the optimal mechanism was known but represented in piecewise forms rather than compact RELU-MLP expressions. Practitioners needed explicit, small-size parametrizations of $h$ that are verifiable (via exact MIP certification) as attaining the conjectured bounds; without such explicit constructions the conjectured tightness of theoretical upper bounds could not be confirmed, and there was no compact, verifiable representation of optimal mechanisms suitable for further theoretical analysis or deployment.

Even when exact certification is possible for tiny networks, a practical measure of success is whether the combined modeling, pruning and training pipeline yields mechanisms that improve or match the state of the art across a range of $n$, and whether ensemble methods can exploit multiple tickets' complementary worst-case profiles. Prior to this work there were limited certified, explicit mechanisms that improved manual baselines for moderate $n$ (e.g., $6\le n\le20$), and it was unknown whether a pruning-and-certify pipeline could systematically produce better certifiable designs at these scales. Without empirical evidence and numerical benchmarks, the community lacked validated techniques for scaling exact worst-case mechanism design beyond the smallest instances.

Many prior neural-network-based mechanism-design studies report worst-case or approximate-guarantee metrics estimated by Monte Carlo sampling. If Monte Carlo estimates can be far from the true global worst case, then training and selection driven by Monte Carlo can produce mechanisms that appear good empirically but violate constraints or degrade dramatically in true worst-case utility. A concrete counterexample demonstrating this inflation was needed to justify the computational overhead of integrating exact MIP certification into the training loop and to argue that reported Monte Carlo numbers cannot be relied upon for worst-case guarantees.

For any fixed number of agents $n$, letting $\alpha^{*}$ denote the optimal worst-case allocative efficiency ratio over all (measurable) VCG redistribution mechanisms, and for any $\epsilon>0$, there exists a VCG redistribution mechanism whose Groves term $h:\{\theta_{-i}\}\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous and whose worst-case allocative efficiency ratio is at least $\alpha^{*}-\epsilon$. Consequently, because the type domain $\{0\le x_1\le x_2\le\cdots\le x_{n-1}\le1\}$ is compact and RELU MLPs can approximate continuous functions on compact domains, RELU multilayer perceptrons are in principle expressive enough to approximate near-optimal VCG redistribution mechanisms arbitrarily closely.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 1 is supported by a rigorous formal proof (Theorem 1, with appendix), which constructs a continuous h approaching the optimal worst-case ratio arbitrarily closely, and by the standard Universal Approximation Theorem that guarantees RELU MLPs can approximate such continuous functions on the compact type domain. No load-bearing weak points were identified; the derivation is mathematically complete and does not rely on uncertain empirical steps. Highlight H7 captures this formal strength. The prior probability is set to 1 because the result is a theorem under the stated assumptions.

nodes.title: Existence of continuous near-optimal Groves term

nodes.content: Given a fixed RELU-activated multilayer perceptron (MLP) parametrization of $h$ (weights and biases treated as constants), the exact worst-case constraint-violation problems on both sides of $(n-1)s(\vec{\theta})\le\sum_i h(\theta_{-i})\le(n-\alpha)s(\vec{\theta})$ can be encoded as mixed-integer programs that (a) maximize the left-side violation $(n-1)s(\vec{\theta})-\sum_i h(\theta_{-i})$, and (b) maximize the right-side violation $\sum_i h(\theta_{-i})-(n-\alpha)s(\vec{\theta})$ with $\alpha$ fixed as a target. Each MIP uses continuous variables for the ordered types $0\le\theta_1\le\cdots\le\theta_n\le1$, auxiliary binaries to model each RELU unit's activation status for each agent (hence one binary per network node per agent), and an auxiliary binary for the $s(\vec\theta)=\max\{\sum_i\theta_i,1\}$ nondifferentiability. The MIPs output $\epsilon_L,\epsilon_R$ (the maximum left/right violation amounts) and corresponding maximizers $\vec\theta_L,\vec\theta_R$ (worst-case type profiles). Given these certified maxima, form $h'(\theta_{-i})=h(\theta_{-i})+\frac{\epsilon_L}{n}$; then $h'$ is guaranteed non-deficit and its provable worst-case allocative efficiency ratio is at least $\alpha-(\epsilon_L+\epsilon_R)$.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 2 describes a standard MIP encoding for piecewise linear functions and an algebraic adjustment formula to produce a feasible mechanism from the MIP outputs. The derivation is routine and does not contain uncertain bridges: the MIP formulation is a straightforward application of mixed-integer modeling with binary variables for RELU activations and for the max function, and the post-processing step follows directly from the inequality manipulation. No load-bearing weak points or distinctive highlights were extracted; the conclusion is credible as a routine methodological statement. The prior probability is set to 0.95 to reflect minor residual uncertainty about the exactness of the encoding (big-M constants not specified), but this does not threaten the existence of such an encoding.

nodes.title: Exact MIP-based worst-case evaluation method for RELU-activated multilayer perceptron Groves term

nodes.content: A practical worst-case training loop (Worst-Case Training, WCT) alternates gradient-based updates on the RELU-activated multilayer perceptron (MLP) $h$ with periodic exact mixed-integer programming (MIP) based worst-case searches; collected worst-case type profiles from the MIPs are incorporated into training batches as hard negative examples. The algorithm uses three training heuristics that improve practical performance: (i) run the costly MIPs only when empirical average loss on a batch (containing latest worst-case profiles, sampled older worst-case profiles, random profiles, and the $n+1$ type profiles in which each agent reports either $0$ or $1/\lceil n/2\rceil$) falls below an adaptive threshold, (ii) revisit and sample from stored older worst-case profiles to prevent oscillation of different worst-case profiles, and (iii) adaptively adjust the training goal $\alpha^G$ via a binary-search style update between a currently-achieved $\alpha^L$ and the theoretical upper bound $\alpha^U$. The algorithm reports and uses the MIP outputs $\epsilon_L,\epsilon_R,\vec\theta_L,\vec\theta_R$; if $\epsilon_L+\epsilon_R\le 0.001$ it advances $\alpha^L$ toward $\alpha^U$.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 3 is subject to premise P1, which identifies that the correctness of the WCT training loop depends on MIPs returning provably optimal constraint violations; without evidence of global optimality, the goal-adjustment mechanism may converge to infeasible or suboptimal mechanisms. Highlight H1 partially offsets this risk by providing a controlled ablation study that shows each of the three training heuristics (including the MIP scheduling) contributes to better empirical worst-case performance across 5 n values with multiple seeds. The ablation demonstrates practical effectiveness, but does not address the theoretical reliance on MIP optimality, because it uses the same MIP process. The residual risk is moderate: the algorithm works well empirically in the tested settings, but the foundational vulnerability remains. The prior probability is 0.7, reflecting the interplay between empirical evidence and computational uncertainty.

nodes.title: Worst-Case Training algorithm (WCT) that integrates MIP certification into training

nodes.content: A lottery-ticket-inspired procedure is introduced to produce tiny RELU subnetworks that are amenable to the mixed-integer programming (MIP) based certification bottleneck: start from a large RELU-activated multilayer perceptron (MLP) with two hidden layers of 20 nodes each, train on random and stored worst-case profiles until loss thresholds, then iteratively prune entire nodes to reach a target ticket size by removing the node with minimum relative importance (importance of a node defined as the sum of absolute outgoing weights, relative importance normalized within its layer). After pruning to the target size, restore the large network to its original initial weights and evaluate the drawn subnetwork by running the Worst-Case Training (WCT) algorithm (up to a fixed budget of MIP rounds); if the drawn ticket fails, save the latest worst-case profiles discovered and use them as part of the training set for the next draw so that subsequent pruning avoids re-drawing the same poor tickets. Repeating draws produces multiple distinct tickets; combining the best two tickets as a randomized ensemble (mixing with probability 0.5) further improves worst-case performance. Empirical ablations show this procedure (Lott.) substantially outperforms simple reinitialization baselines that either (a) directly initialize small networks (Reinit1), (b) reset initializations without sharing worst-case profiles (Reinit2), or (c) reuse the same initialization (Reinit0).

metadata.narrative: Premise P2 notes that the pruning heuristic (outgoing-weight sum) lacks theoretical justification and has limited empirical validation. Highlights H2 and H3 provide strong empirical counterweights: H2 shows that the lottery-ticket pipeline (Lott.) outperforms three reinitialization baselines across all tested n and ticket sizes in a controlled 10-draw comparison, and H3 demonstrates that the algorithm generates new and improving tickets for n=8. While the heuristic's theoretical basis is weak, the empirical evidence covers multiple n values, multiple seeds, and concrete ticket-draw statistics, suggesting that for the tested domain (n≤10, 10–20 draws), the heuristic is effective. The risk from P2 is mitigated within this domain, but extrapolation to larger n or to different mechanism design settings is unprotected. The prior probability is 0.75, reflecting the strong but bounded empirical support.

nodes.title: Lottery Ticket motivated pipeline for finding tiny trainable RELU subnetworks

metadata.narrative: Premise P3 identifies that the MIP certification used to claim near-optimality for the n=4 and n=5 mechanisms does not document solver optimality status, so the reported gaps might be optimistic. Highlight H4 counters that the explicit, high-precision weight matrices are provided, enabling independent re-certification, and the reported gaps are very small (5.8e-5 for n=5). If the MIPs are indeed globally optimal, the conclusion is fully supported; if not, the explicit weights allow the community to verify or tighten the claim. The interaction is partially offsetting: the highlight provides the means to independently address the weak point, but the paper itself does not resolve the uncertainty. The prior probability of 0.70 reflects that the claim is likely correct (the gaps are very small and the MIP instances are small) but not formally confirmed in the paper.

nodes.title: Explicit (near-)optimal Groves terms found for small n (3,4,5)

nodes.content: Applying the lottery-ticket pipeline plus the Worst-Case Training (WCT) algorithm and mixed-integer programming (MIP) certification produced mechanisms that substantially improve the best previously-known manual worst-case gaps for a range of $n$ and are certifiably better when evaluated exactly by MIP. Representative certified results include: for $n\in\{6,7,8,9,10\}$ the best single-ticket gaps to the theoretical upper bound (Lott.) are 0.1541 (n=6), 0.0364 (n=7), 0.0629 (n=8), 0.0845 (n=9), 0.1929 (n=10) while randomized ensembles of the two best tickets further reduced gaps to 0.1531, 0.0354, 0.0621, 0.0837, 0.1924 respectively. For larger $n$ up to 20, with ticket size 6 the algorithm produces certifiably better mechanisms than manual baselines; examples include n=12 gap 0.1690 vs manual 0.2537, n=14 gap 0.2767 vs manual 0.3560, n=20 gap 0.2903 vs manual 0.3124. Empirical ablations demonstrate that the lottery drawing procedure produces better tickets than several reinitialization baselines; the ensemble of top tickets often yields the best certified worst-case performance.

metadata.narrative: Premise P4 raises the same MIP optimality concern for the gaps reported in Tables 3 and 4 across all n from 6 to 20; if the MIPs were not globally solved, the reported improvements over manual baselines could be optimistic. Highlight H5 shows that the improvements are large and consistent across 11 n values, with the Lott. gap better than the manual baseline in every case. The magnitude and consistency of the improvements make it unlikely that all improvements are artifacts of MIP suboptimality, but the threat is not preempted—the same certification method is used for all data points. The conclusion's credibility rests on the plausible assumption that the MIPs were solved to sufficient quality to preserve the ranking, but the absence of optimality documentation leaves a significant residual risk. The prior probability is 0.65, reflecting the tension between strong empirical patterns and an unverified computational foundation.

nodes.title: Empirical improvements and certified results up to 20 agents, and ensemble benefits

nodes.content: Empirically, Monte Carlo sampling can substantially overestimate worst-case allocative efficiency. As an explicit example, a mechanism found for $n=10$ attains a worst-case allocative efficiency ratio of $0.685$ when evaluated exactly via the mixed-integer programming (MIP) certification procedure, whereas Monte Carlo evaluation over 10,000 random type profiles reports an inflated ratio of $0.765$. This quantifies the potential magnitude of Monte Carlo optimism in this setting and motivates the use of exact worst-case MIP certification during training and evaluation.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 7 is supported by a single concrete example (n=10) where Monte Carlo overestimates the worst-case ratio by 0.08 (0.765 vs 0.685 via MIP). No weak points were identified: the example is specific, the comparison is clear, and the claim (that Monte Carlo can be optimistic) does not require universality. Highlight H6 captures this illustrative evidence. The prior probability is set to 0.9 because the example is convincing for the existence claim, though the magnitude of average overestimation in other settings is not quantified.

nodes.title: Demonstration that Monte Carlo worst-case estimation is overly optimistic (example) and need for exact certification

nodes.content: In the Worst-Case Training (WCT) algorithm, the mixed-integer programs (MIPs) that compute the maximum left-side violation $\epsilon_L = \max_{\vec{\theta}} (n-1)s(\vec{\theta}) - \sum_i h(\theta_{-i})$ and the maximum right-side violation $\epsilon_R = \max_{\vec{\theta}} \sum_i h(\theta_{-i}) - (n-\alpha^G)s(\vec{\theta})$ for a fixed RELU-activated multilayer perceptron (MLP) $h$ must be solved to global optimality. Each MIP uses one binary variable per RELU node per agent (up to 20 agents and 20 nodes) and treats $h$'s weights as constants. No evidence is provided that the employed MIP solver achieves proven global optimality for these instances within the allocated compute time; if the solver returns a feasible solution whose objective is not provably the global maximum, the resulting $\epsilon$ values are lower bounds on the true maximum violation. The algorithm then uses these under-estimated $\epsilon$ values in the condition $\epsilon_L+\epsilon_R \le 0.001$ to decide whether to advance the training goal $\alpha^G$ toward the theoretical upper bound $\alpha^U$. If the condition is met erroneously, the goal advances prematurely toward an infeasible target, causing the subsequently trained $h$ to fail the non-deficit constraint and degrading the certified worst-case ratio.

metadata.failure_mode: If the MIP solver fails to prove global optimality for any call during training and returns an epsilon that is a strict lower bound on the true maximum violation, then the condition epsilon_L+epsilon_R ≤ 0.001 may be satisfied even though the current h is farther from feasibility than measured. The algorithm then raises α^G to a value that the network cannot actually achieve given the true violation landscape. Subsequent gradient-based training attempts to meet the infeasible goal, resulting in a final h that violates the non-deficit constraint or whose certified worst-case ratio is strictly worse than the reported α^G - (epsilon_L+epsilon_R). The conclusion that WCT is a "practical worst-case training loop" that validly integrates MIP certification is undermined because the correctness of the loop depends on the MIP outputs being global optima.
metadata.weakness_reason: The correctness of the MIP encoding is not in doubt, but the reliability of the solver's output depends on whether it can prove global optimality for each instance. For problem sizes typical of the experiments (n up to 20, network nodes up to 20, binary variables up to 400), state-of-the-art MIP solvers can often solve to optimality, but this is not guaranteed—the paper does not report solve times, optimality gaps, or termination statuses. Without this information, the reader cannot confirm that the epsilon values used in training are indeed global maxima, and thus cannot confirm that the mechanism h' = h+epsilon_L/n satisfies the constraints and achieves the claimed worst-case ratio.

nodes.title: MIP global optimality not verified in WCT

nodes.content: In the lottery-ticket pipeline, subnetworks are pruned from a large pre-trained network (e.g., a RELU-activated multilayer perceptron (MLP) with two hidden layers of 20 nodes each) to a target small size by repeatedly removing the node with the minimum relative importance, defined as the node's outgoing-weight sum of absolute values divided by the total outgoing-weight sum of its layer. This pruning criterion is not derived from any known property of the worst-case VCG redistribution mechanism design objective, nor is it justified by the theoretical lottery ticket literature (which typically uses iterative magnitude pruning with weight rewinding). No theoretical argument is provided that pruning based on outgoing-weight magnitude, performed during training when the loss is below a threshold, preserves the trainability properties that make a small subnetwork a 'winning ticket' for the specific optimization landscape of the Worst-Case Training (WCT) algorithm. The empirical validation of the heuristic is limited to n values 6–10 with 10 draws each and a single detailed analysis for n=8; beyond these settings (e.g., n>10, different large-network architectures) the effectiveness is unsubstantiated.

metadata.failure_mode: If the pruning heuristic does not reliably select subnetworks that are "trainable" (i.e., that can achieve low WCT loss after modally 100 MIP rounds), then many draws will produce tickets that fail to improve the worst-case gap, and the pipeline may not find any winning ticket within a practical number of draws. The conclusion that Algorithm 2 provides a "principled way to obtain tiny trainable RELU subnetworks" for this task would be false; the pipeline would be reduced to an inefficient trial-and-error process no better than random reinitialization, and the empirical results in Tables 3 and 4 could be overfitted to the specific random draws that happened to produce good tickets.
metadata.weakness_reason: The lottery ticket hypothesis states that large randomly initialized networks contain sparse subnetworks that train to comparable accuracy when reset to their initial weights, but the standard method for identifying such tickets is iterative magnitude pruning with rewinding. Here, nodes are pruned one at a time during training without weight rewinding, and the importance metric (outgoing-weight sum) is not the metric used in the standard ticket-finding literature. There is no theoretical or empirical reason that this particular criterion selects subnetworks that are especially trainable for the worst-case mechanism design objective; the connection to the hypothesis is purely inspirational. The ablation study (Table 2) does demonstrate superiority over reinitialization baselines for n=6–10, but this is a limited regime, and the heuristic's reliability beyond n=10 or with different large-network initialization distributions is unknown.

nodes.title: Pruning heuristic lacks theoretical justification and limited validation

nodes.content: For the explicit RELU-activated multilayer perceptron (MLP) Groves terms claimed to be near-optimal for n=4 (5 hidden nodes) and n=5 (20 hidden nodes), it is reported that the mixed-integer programming (MIP) certified worst-case allocative efficiency gap to the conjectured theoretical upper bound is at most $5.8159\times 10^{-5}$ for n=5 and effectively zero (within floating point) for n=4. The MIP solver's termination status for these certification runs is not documented: it is not stated whether the solver proved global optimality of the returned epsilon values, whether a time limit was imposed, or what optimality gap (if any) was reported at termination. Consequently, the reader cannot determine whether the reported epsilon values are provably the global maxima or merely feasible solutions that may underestimate the true worst-case violation. If the solver did not prove global optimality, the actual worst-case ratio of the published mechanism could be strictly lower (i.e., a larger gap from the upper bound) than the stated value, and the conclusion that the conjectured upper bounds are tight for n=4 and n=5 as confirmed by these numbers would be unconfirmed.

metadata.failure_mode: If the MIP solver did not prove global optimality and the returned epsilon_L+epsilon_R is only a lower bound on the true maximum violation, then the true worst-case gap from the theoretical upper bound may be larger than 5.8159e-05 (and possibly large enough to invalidate the claim of near-optimality). The conclusion that the conjectured upper bounds are tight for n=4 and n=5 (as confirmed by these explicit mechanisms) would be unsupported; the mechanisms may not actually attain the claimed performance, and the result would revert to the previous state where tightness was unresolved. The failure is specific and load-bearing because the entire claim of optimal or near-optimal discovery for n=4 and n=5 depends on these certified gaps.
metadata.weakness_reason: The use of MIP to certify worst-case performance is sound in principle, but the trustworthiness of the results depends on whether the solver achieves provable optimality. For a relatively small MIP (e.g., 20 binary variables for n=4 with 5 hidden nodes, or 100 binary variables for n=5 with 20 hidden nodes) and a linear objective, it is likely that a modern solver can solve to optimality within seconds, but the paper provides no information to confirm this. The absence of any optimality gap or solver status is a significant omission because the claim of near-optimality rests entirely on these epsilon numbers; if the MIP was terminated pre-optimally, the claim is not supported.

nodes.title: Near-optimality certification status not documented

nodes.content: For the best lottery-ticket mechanisms reported for n=6..10 and n=12..20, the worst-case gaps to the theoretical upper bound are obtained by solving mixed-integer programs (MIPs) for left and right constraint violations on the final $h$ functions. The MIP solver's termination status (proven optimal, feasible with gap, time limit) is not documented for any of these certification runs. If the solver terminated without proving global optimality, the reported $\epsilon_L+\epsilon_R$ may be lower than the true maximum violation, leading to reported gaps that are optimistic (too low). Consequently, the claimed improvements over manual baselines could be invalid or smaller than stated.

metadata.failure_mode: If the MIPs used to compute the gaps in Tables 3 and 4 did not prove global optimality, the reported gaps are lower bounds on the true gaps; the true worst-case ratios may be worse than stated. The conclusion that the lottery-ticket pipeline produces mechanisms that "substantially improve the best previously-known manual worst-case gaps" would be weakened or invalidated, because the comparison uses the reported (possibly optimistic) gaps against the manual gaps (which are presumably exact or analytically derived). The specific quantitative figures in the tables would no longer be credible.
metadata.weakness_reason: Same rationale as P1 and P3: the paper does not provide any evidence that the MIPs used to certify the final mechanisms in Tables 3 and 4 achieved global optimality. Given the larger problem instances (up to 20 agents and up to 20 nodes, i.e., up to 400 binary variables plus auxiliary variables) and the tighter time budgets (evaluation of ensemble took hours for some n), it is plausible that some MIPs were run with a time limit and returned suboptimal solutions. Without solver logs or optimality gap reporting, the reliability of the numerical claims rests on an unverified computational assumption.

nodes.title: MIP global optimality not verified for reported lottery-ticket mechanisms

nodes.content: For n=6 through n=10, with a fixed network size of [10,10] and 5 random seeds per configuration, the Worst-Case Training algorithm (WCT) that runs MIPs only when the average loss is below a threshold, revisits old worst-case profiles, and adaptively adjusts the training goal (binary search between α^L and α^U) is compared against three ablated variants: WCT-1 (MIPs run even when loss high), WCT-2 (no revisit of old profiles), and WCT-3 (goal fixed at the theoretical upper bound). Each variant receives 1 hour of compute per seed. For each n, the average gap to the theoretical upper bound and the minimum gap across the 5 seeds are reported. WCT achieves the smallest average gap for n=6, 9, and 10, and the smallest minimum gap for n=6, 8, 9, and 10, and is a close second for the remaining entries, dominating the ablated variants over the tested range (Table 1).

metadata.credit: This controlled ablation study preempts the failure mode in which the three training heuristics are arbitrary and non-contributing: by comparing WCT to three variants each lacking one heuristic, the paper provides specific evidence that each heuristic improves worst-case performance, justifying their inclusion in the algorithm. The use of multiple n values, multiple seeds per n, and a fixed computational budget ensures that the comparison is fair and that the observed advantages are not due to overfitting to a single configuration. Without this study, the heuristics would be supported only by intuition; with it, the conclusion that WCT is a "practical" training algorithm that effectively integrates MIP certification is substantially more credible because the component-level contributions are separately validated.

nodes.title: Controlled ablation study of WCT heuristics

nodes.content: For n=6 through n=10 and for ticket sizes 10 and 20, the lottery-ticket pipeline (Lott., Algorithm 2) is compared against three reinitialization baselines: Reinit0 (same initialization every draw, no shared worst-case profiles), Reinit1 (random reinitialization, same architecture as the target subnetwork), and Reinit2 (random reinitialization, with shared worst-case profiles across draws). Each setting runs 10 draws; the minimum gap to the theoretical upper bound across draws is recorded. Lott. produces the lowest gap in all 10 combinations of n and ticket size (Table 2).

metadata.credit: This systematic comparison preempts the failure mode in which the pruning-based ticket finding offers no advantage over simpler methods: by including three baselines that vary both the initialization strategy and the use of historical worst-case profiles, the paper shows that the pruning heuristic itself, combined with profile sharing, is responsible for the improvement, not merely the extra data or the number of draws. The consistent dominance across 10 configurations (5 n values × 2 sizes) provides strong empirical support for the claim that Algorithm 2 produces tiny trainable subnetworks. Without this comparison, the lottery-ticket pipeline would be a black-box procedure with unsubstantiated benefit; with it, its advantage over straightforward reinitialization is quantitatively established for the tested domain.

nodes.title: Controlled comparison of Lott. vs reinitialization baselines

nodes.content: For n=8 agents, the lottery-ticket pipeline (Algorithm 2) was executed with six target ticket sizes (10,12,14,16,18,20) for 24 hours per size. Across all draws, 78% of the subnetworks obtained are distinct from all previously drawn subnetworks (i.e., new tickets), and 88% of draws produce a subnetwork whose WCT-based certified worst-case gap is strictly better than that of any previously drawn subnetwork (Figure 1).

metadata.credit: This analysis directly supports the key claim of Algorithm 2: that the mechanism of storing worst-case type profiles from failed tickets and using them to guide future pruning reliably generates new tickets and successively better ones. The failure mode preempted is that the algorithm would repeatedly draw the same bad tickets or fail to find improving ones, making the pipeline wasteful. The empirical demonstration that 78% are new and 88% are improvements shows the algorithm is fulfilling its designed function. Without this analysis, the claim of systematic ticket improvement would be speculative; with it, the mechanism is validated for the n=8 case, and the approach is more credible for other n as well.

nodes.title: Ticket diversity and improvement analysis

nodes.content: The paper publishes the complete set of RELU MLP weights and biases for an h function for n=4 agents with 5 hidden nodes (coefficients given to 8 significant digits) and for n=5 agents with 20 hidden nodes (coefficients given to 8 significant digits). The MIP certification run on these h functions reports a total violation epsilon_L+epsilon_R corresponding to a worst-case efficiency gap from the conjectured theoretical upper bound of at most 5.8159×10^{-5} for n=5 and effectively zero (within MIP tolerances) for n=4. Additionally, for n=3 the paper provides six distinct optimal h functions in compact RELU form (e.g., 2–3 hidden nodes). These explicit representations allow any researcher to reconstruct the mechanisms exactly, to re-run the MIP certification independently, and to verify the claimed gaps.

metadata.credit: This highlight preempts the failure mode in which the claimed near-optimal results are not reproducible or are only claimed without demonstration: by providing the actual numerical parameters, the paper enables independent verification of the worst-case gaps. The high precision and small reported gaps provide strong numerical evidence that the conjectured upper bounds are tight for n=4 and n=5, resolving an open question. Without this explicit provision, the conclusion would be a bare claim of having found near-optimal mechanisms; with it, the community can inspect, test, and potentially prove optimality analytically. The scope of credit is that the qualitative and quantitative layers of the conclusion (that the upper bounds are attainable) are underwritten by checkable numerical evidence.

nodes.title: Explicit near-optimal mechanisms with high precision weights and MIP gaps

nodes.content: Using the lottery-ticket pipeline (Algorithm 2) combined with WCT (Algorithm 1) and MIP certification, the paper reports the best single-ticket (Lott.) and two-ticket ensemble gaps to the theoretical upper bound for n=6,7,8,9,10 (Table 3) and for n=12,14,16,18,20 with ticket size 6 (Table 4). For every n listed, the Lott. gap is strictly smaller than the best manual baseline reported in prior literature (e.g., [15]), and the ensemble gap further reduces the gap for n=6..10. Representative improvements: n=7 gap reduces from 0.1766 (manual) to 0.0364 (Lott.); n=12 from 0.2537 to 0.1690; n=20 from 0.3124 to 0.2903.

metadata.credit: This highlight provides direct empirical evidence that the integrated pipeline (lottery ticket, WCT, MIP certification) produces mechanisms that improve over the state of the art across a wide range of n, up to at least 20 agents. The failure mode preempted is that the approach might work only for very small n (3,4,5) or that the improvements over manual designs are marginal or non-existent. The comprehensive coverage (11 n values, each with a manual baseline) shows consistent improvement, often substantial. The results underwrite the conclusion's quantitative layer (the magnitude of improvement) and its generalization/extrapolation scope (the approach scales to n=20). Without this empirical sweep, the claim of "substantially improved worst-case mechanisms" would be based only on a few favourable examples; with it, the claim is quantitatively supported across the tested range.

nodes.title: Comprehensive empirical improvements over manual baselines across n=6..20

nodes.content: For a specific VCG redistribution mechanism for n=10 agents obtained from the training pipeline, the worst-case allocative efficiency ratio is computed by exact MIP certification (using the method described in the paper) as 0.685, and by Monte Carlo evaluation over 10,000 random type profiles as 0.765. The Monte Carlo estimate is 0.08 higher (approximately 12% relative overestimation). The comparison is reported in the paper without further details on the sampling distribution or the specific mechanism used.

metadata.credit: This concrete numerical example preempts the failure mode in which the claim that Monte Carlo worst-case estimation is overly optimistic is merely theoretical or not quantified in this domain. By showing an instance where Monte Carlo overestimates by 0.08, the paper demonstrates that the inflation can be large enough to materially misrepresent the mechanism's true worst-case performance. Without this example, the motivation for using computationally expensive MIP certification would be weaker; with it, readers can see the tangible gap and understand why exact certification is necessary for trustable worst-case guarantees. The example supports the conclusion's qualitative direction (Monte Carlo can be optimistic) and provides a ballpark magnitude for the inflation.

nodes.title: Concrete quantification of Monte Carlo optimism

nodes.content: Theorem 1: For any constant number of agents n, let α* be the optimal worst-case allocative efficiency ratio (the supremum over all measurable VCG redistribution mechanisms). For any ε>0, there exists a VCG redistribution mechanism whose Groves term h is continuous and whose worst-case allocative efficiency ratio is at least α*-ε. The proof proceeds by discretizing [0,1] into L equal intervals, randomly rounding each input coordinate to an interval endpoint with probability proportional to its distance, defining h^L as the expected value of an optimal h* under this random rounding, showing that h^L is Lipschitz and satisfies modified constraints, and then scaling it to obtain h' that satisfies the original constraints with ratio α* - O(n/L). By choosing L large enough, the O(n/L) term can be made smaller than ε. The domain {0≤x_1≤...≤x_{n-1}≤1} is compact, so the Universal Approximation Theorem implies that RELU MLPs can approximate such continuous functions arbitrarily closely.

metadata.credit: The formal proof of Theorem 1 directly preempts the failure mode that the optimal mechanisms might be discontinuous, making RELU MLP representation inadequate. The construction provides a theoretically grounded guarantee that, for any grove of optimality, there is a continuous h that gets arbitrarily close. Without this theorem, the paper's entire approach of searching over continuous RELU networks would rest on an untested assumption; with it, the Universal Approximation Theorem can be applied and the neural-network search is justified in principle. The proof is rigorous, self-contained, and does not rely on external assumptions beyond the standard mechanism model. The scope of credit: the conclusion that RELU MLPs are in principle expressive enough to approximate near-optimal mechanisms is fully underwritten by this formal guarantee.

nodes.title: Theorem 1: constructive existence of continuous near-optimal h

steps.reasoning: Define the basic problem context and notation used throughout the derivation: let $n$ be the number of agents (treated as a constant), $\vec{\theta}=(\theta_1,\theta_2,\dots,\theta_n)$ denote a type profile with each agent's type satisfying $0\le \theta_i\le 1$, $s(\vec{\theta})=\max\{\sum_i \theta_i,1\}$ denote the first-best total utility under efficient allocation, and let $\alpha^{*}$ denote the optimal worst-case allocative efficiency ratio over all (measurable) VCG redistribution (Groves) mechanisms.

State the design-objective inequality that characterizes feasibility of a Groves term $h$: for all $\vec{\theta}$, the mechanism must satisfy $(n-1)s(\vec{\theta}) \le \sum_i h(\theta_{-i}) \le (n-\alpha) s(\vec{\theta})$, where $\theta_{-i}$ denotes the vector of all agents' types except agent $i$, and $\alpha$ is the mechanism's worst-case allocative efficiency ratio (this inequality is the paper's single constraint summarizing non-deficit and approximation objectives).

Let $h^{*}$ denote an optimal (possibly discontinuous or measurable) Groves term achieving worst-case ratio $\alpha^{*}$; the goal is to construct a continuous $h$ that attains worst-case ratio arbitrarily close to $\alpha^{*}$.

Introduce a discretization grid parameter $L\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}$ (a large integer). Partition the interval $[0,1]$ into $L$ equal subintervals $[0,\tfrac{1}{L}], [\tfrac{1}{L},\tfrac{2}{L}],\dots, [\tfrac{L-1}{L},1]$. This $L$ will later be sent large to make approximation error small.

Define a randomized rounding operator on each coordinate: for any coordinate value $x\in[0,1]$ that lies in the grid interval $[\tfrac{k}{L},\tfrac{k+1}{L}]$, round $x$ down to $\tfrac{k}{L}$ with probability $(\tfrac{k+1}{L}-x)/(1/L)$ and round $x$ up to $\tfrac{k+1}{L}$ with probability $(x-\tfrac{k}{L})/(1/L)$; do this rounding independently (conceptually) for every input coordinate.

Define $h^{L}$ as the expectation of $h^{*}$ under the above randomized rounding applied to all $n-1$ inputs: that is, for input $(x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})$, consider the $2^{n-1}$ grid points obtained by rounding each $x_i$ either down or up, evaluate $h^{*}$ on each grid point, and take the weighted sum with weights equal to the rounding probabilities; thus $h^{L}(x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})$ is a weighted average of $h^{*}$'s values on grid points.

Argue continuity of $h^{L}$: because $h^{L}$ is a finite weighted sum of the values of $h^{*}$ at finitely many grid points and the weights depend continuously on the inputs $(x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})$, the map $(x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})\mapsto h^{L}(x_1,\dots,x_{n-1})$ is continuous. (The paper notes Lipschitz continuity follows similarly because the grid is finite.)

Show that $h^{L}$ approximately preserves the mechanism inequalities satisfied by $h^{*}$ on the continuous domain, but with small additive slack proportional to $n/L$: because $h^{*}$ satisfies $(n-1)s(\vec{\theta}) \le \sum_i h^{*}(\theta_{-i}) \le (n-\alpha^{*}) s(\vec{\theta})$ for every $\vec{\theta}$ including all grid points, applying the randomized rounding construction yields, for every $\vec{\theta}$,
$(n-1)\max\{\sum_i \theta_i - \tfrac{n}{L},1\} \le \sum_i h^{L}(\theta_{-i}) \le (n-\alpha^{*})\max\{\sum_i \theta_i + \tfrac{n}{L},1\}$,
because each coordinate rounding can change each agent-sum by at most $\tfrac{1}{L}$ and there are $n$ agents appearing across the $n$ terms $\theta_{-i}$.

Simplify the previous bounds using $s(\vec{\theta})=\max\{\sum_i\theta_i,1\}$ and the fact that $s(\vec{\theta})\ge 1$, yielding
$(n-1)(s(\vec{\theta})-\tfrac{n}{L}) \le \sum_i h^{L}(\theta_{-i}) \le (n-\alpha^{*})(s(\vec{\theta})+\tfrac{n}{L})$ for all $\vec{\theta}$.

Remove the left-side fractional deficit by scaling up $h^{L}$: define $h'(\,\cdot\,)=\dfrac{h^{L}( \,\cdot\,)}{1-\tfrac{n}{L}}$. Because $1-\tfrac{n}{L}>0$ for sufficiently large $L$, $h'$ remains continuous and the left inequality becomes $(n-1)s(\vec{\theta})\le \sum_i h'(\theta_{-i})$ for all $\vec{\theta}$.

Bound the right-side after scaling: substituting $h'=h^{L}/(1-\tfrac{n}{L})$ into the right inequality gives for all $\vec{\theta}$
$\sum_i h'(\theta_{-i}) \le (n-\alpha^{*})\dfrac{1+\tfrac{n}{L}}{1-\tfrac{n}{L}} \, s(\vec{\theta})$.

Convert the multiplicative slack on the right-hand side into an additive degradation of the worst-case allocative efficiency ratio: observe that for any desired $\epsilon>0$, choose $L$ large enough so that $(n-\alpha^{*})\dfrac{1+\tfrac{n}{L}}{1-\tfrac{n}{L}} \le n - (\alpha^{*}-\epsilon)$; rearranging shows that the continuous $h'$ satisfies $(n-1)s(\vec{\theta}) \le \sum_i h'(\theta_{-i}) \le (n-(\alpha^{*}-\epsilon)) s(\vec{\theta})$ for every $\vec{\theta}$.

Conclude the existence statement: for any $\epsilon>0$, constructing $h'$ as above yields a continuous Groves term whose worst-case allocative efficiency ratio is at least $\alpha^{*}-\epsilon$, thereby proving the main claim that continuous Groves terms can be arbitrarily close to the optimal measurable $\alpha^{*}$ for fixed $n$.

Argue that RELU multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) can in principle approximate such continuous $h'$ arbitrarily well on the relevant domain: first note the domain of $h'$ is $\{0\le x_1\le x_2\le\cdots\le x_{n-1}\le 1\}$, which is a closed and bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ and therefore compact; invoke the universal approximation statement from prior work that continuous functions on compact domains can be arbitrarily approximated by appropriate MLP architectures with suitable activation functions (the paper cites a theorem from [19] for the single-layer continuous-bounded-nonconstant activation case and then argues RELU is applicable).
[19]

Explain why RELU is an admissible activation for the cited universal-approximation result: show that a continuous, bounded, non-constant "spike" function can be written as a linear combination of three RELUs via $\psi(x)=\operatorname{RELU}(x-1)-2\operatorname{RELU}(x)+\operatorname{RELU}(x+1)$; therefore RELU-based MLPs (with enough nodes/layers) lie within the class characterized by the universal approximation theorem and can approximate any continuous target such as $h'$ on the compact input domain.

Combine the above conclusions: since for any $\epsilon>0$ there exists a continuous $h'$ with worst-case ratio at least $\alpha^{*}-\epsilon$, and since RELU MLPs can approximate continuous functions on the compact, ordered-domain arbitrarily well, RELU MLPs are in principle expressive enough to approximate near-optimal VCG redistribution mechanisms arbitrarily closely for any fixed $n$.
[19]

Set up the evaluation objective and notation: given a fixed RELU-activated multilayer perceptron (MLP) parametrization of the Groves term $h$ (i.e., the network architecture and all weights and biases are treated as constants), recall the mechanism feasibility inequality for all type profiles $\vec{\theta}$,
$(n-1)s(\vec{\theta}) \le \sum_i h(\theta_{-i}) \le (n-\alpha) s(\vec{\theta})$,
where $s(\vec{\theta})=\max\{\sum_i \theta_i,1\}$ and $\alpha$ is a target worst-case allocative efficiency ratio to be tested.

Formulate the two scalar worst-case violation objectives that certify feasibility for the given $h$: (a) the maximal left-side violation amount is $\epsilon_L = \max_{\vec{\theta}} \big\{(n-1)s(\vec{\theta}) - \sum_i h(\theta_{-i})\big\}$, and (b) the maximal right-side violation amount (for fixed $\alpha$) is $\epsilon_R = \max_{\vec{\theta}} \big\{\sum_i h(\theta_{-i}) - (n-\alpha) s(\vec{\theta})\big\}$. If both maxima are non-positive, $h$ satisfies the inequality for all $\vec{\theta}$ with the given $\alpha$.

Encode each maximization as a mixed-integer program (MIP) by introducing variables and constraints that model the network computation and the nondifferentiable $s$ function: include continuous decision variables $\theta_1,\theta_2,\dots,\theta_n$ constrained to satisfy $0\le\theta_1\le\theta_2\le\cdots\le\theta_n\le 1$ (the paper assumes without loss of generality sorted types and sorted inputs to $h$), include linear constraints representing each affine pre-activation in the RELU MLP, and introduce auxiliary binary variables to model activation status for each RELU unit per agent (that is, one binary per network node per agent) so that the piecewise-linear RELU behavior is captured exactly within the MIP.

Model the nondifferentiability of $s(\vec{\theta})=\max\{\sum_i\theta_i,1\}$ by introducing an additional auxiliary binary variable that selects whether $\sum_i\theta_i\ge 1$ or not, together with linear constraints that enforce $s(\vec{\theta})$ equals the appropriate branch; this binary ensures exact handling of the $s$ function in the MIP optimization.

Summarize the MIP outputs and their interpretations: solving the left-side MIP yields the maximizer type profile $\vec{\theta}_L$ and the maximum left violation $\epsilon_L$, and solving the right-side MIP (with $\alpha$ fixed) yields $\vec{\theta}_R$ and $\epsilon_R$; these values are certified maxima because the MIPs encode the exact piecewise-linear network and exact $s(\vec{\theta})$ logic.

Translate the certified maxima into uniform bounding inequalities valid for all $\vec{\theta}$: because $\epsilon_L$ and $\epsilon_R$ are the maximum violation amounts, they guarantee
$\forall \vec{\theta},\quad (n-1)s(\vec{\theta}) - \epsilon_L \le \sum_i h(\theta_{-i}) \le (n-\alpha) s(\vec{\theta}) + \epsilon_R$,
i.e., $h$ may violate the desired inequality by at most $\epsilon_L$ on the left and $\epsilon_R$ on the right for any profile.

Construct a certified, non-deficit Groves term $h'$ from $h$ and the left violation certificate: define $h'(\theta_{-i}) = h(\theta_{-i}) + \dfrac{\epsilon_L}{n}$. Note that $h'$ is obtained by adding the uniform constant $\epsilon_L/n$ to each agent's redistribution term, which increases the sum $\sum_i h'(\theta_{-i})$ by exactly $\epsilon_L$ for every profile.

Prove that $h'$ is non-deficit (i.e., satisfies the left inequality exactly): substituting $h'$ into the left inequality from Step 6 gives $(n-1)s(\vec{\theta}) \le \sum_i h'(\theta_{-i})$ because the $-\epsilon_L$ slack in Step 6 is compensated by adding $\epsilon_L$ across agents; this uses only the fact that the MIP output $\epsilon_L$ is the maximal left-side violation of the original $h$.

Derive a provable lower bound on $h'$'s worst-case allocative efficiency ratio using the right-side bound: substituting $h'$ into the right inequality from Step 6 yields $\sum_i h'(\theta_{-i}) \le (n-\alpha) s(\vec{\theta}) + \epsilon_R + \epsilon_L$. Because $s(\vec{\theta})\ge 1$, rearrange to conclude that $h'$ achieves a worst-case allocative efficiency ratio of at least $\alpha - (\epsilon_L+\epsilon_R)$ (equivalently, the mechanism specified by $h'$ satisfies $(n-1)s(\vec{\theta}) \le \sum_i h'(\theta_{-i}) \le (n-(\alpha-(\epsilon_L+\epsilon_R))) s(\vec{\theta})$ for all $\vec{\theta}$).

Record computational remarks and scaling properties indicated by the paper: each MIP requires one binary variable per network node per agent plus one binary for $s(\vec{\theta})$, so the MIP encodings are exact but scale poorly with network size and number of agents; the method nevertheless yields certified maximizers $\vec{\theta}_L,\vec{\theta}_R$ and certified violation amounts $\epsilon_L,\epsilon_R$ that can be used both for evaluation and as hard negatives in training.
[4]

Start from known upstream results: use the existence of continuous near-optimal Groves terms and the fact that RELU MLPs can approximate continuous $h$ arbitrarily well (established in Conclusion 1) and use the exact MIP-based worst-case evaluation/certification procedure for a fixed RELU MLP $h$ (established in Conclusion 2) as primitives that the algorithm integrates into training.

Outline the high-level structure of the Worst-Case Training (WCT) algorithm: alternate gradient-based updates (Adam SGD) on the RELU-MLP parameterizing $h$ with periodic exact MIP-based worst-case searches that compute $\epsilon_L,\epsilon_R,\vec{\theta}_L,\vec{\theta}_R$ for the current $h$, collect the MIP-found worst-case type profiles into a stored pool WCP, and include these worst-case profiles as hard negative examples in subsequent training batches to reduce worst-case violations.

Detail the composition of each training batch used during SGD: each training batch contains (i) 16 latest calculated worst-case type profiles (the most recent entries from WCP), (ii) 16 randomly sampled older worst-case profiles from WCP (to revisit previous worst cases), (iii) 16 random type profiles drawn according to the paper's specified sampling distribution (with one-third chance of drawing 0, one-third chance of drawing $1/\lceil n/2\rceil$, and one-third chance from $U(0,1)$), and (iv) $n+1$ special profiles where agents report either $0$ or $1/\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ used in deriving the theoretical upper bound; these are concatenated as the batch on which SGD runs for a fixed number of epochs.

Explain the periodic exact MIP calls and how their outputs are used in training: after SGD epochs, conditional on a training criterion, two MIPs (left and right violation maximizations) are solved with the current network parameters treated as constants to obtain $\epsilon_L,\epsilon_R,\vec{\theta}_L,\vec{\theta}_R$, and the obtained worst-case profiles $\vec{\theta}_L,\vec{\theta}_R$ are appended to WCP for future batches; the network to be delivered at the end of training is $h'(\cdot)=h(\cdot)+\epsilon_L/n$ as in the MIP-certification derivation so the final mechanism is guaranteed non-deficit and its provable worst-case ratio is at least $\alpha - (\epsilon_L+\epsilon_R)$.

State the three practical training heuristics (the criteria that improve practical performance) precisely:
(i) Run the costly MIPs only when necessary: compute the empirical average loss over a block of SGD epochs; if the average loss remains above an adaptive threshold (the threshold increases over time according to a schedule described in the implementation details, specifically incrementing by $0.0001\cdot 2^{\lceil k/10\rceil}$ after $k$ repetitions without MIP), skip MIP calls and continue SGD because random sampling is likely to find violations when loss is large.
(ii) Revisit stored older worst-case profiles: include randomly sampled older WCP entries in training batches so previous worst-case profiles are re-exposed to the network and to prevent "whac-a-mole" oscillation where fixing one profile creates a new worst case elsewhere.
(iii) Adaptively adjust the training goal $\alpha^G$: maintain $\alpha^L$ (the best achieved certified ratio so far) and the theoretical upper bound $\alpha^U$; set a working training goal $\alpha^G$ and update it in a binary-search-style based on whether MIP outputs satisfy $\epsilon_L + \epsilon_R \le 0.001$ (if so, advance $\alpha^G$ toward $\alpha^U$ by setting $\alpha^L=\alpha^G$ and $\alpha^G=(\alpha^U+\alpha^G)/2$, otherwise reduce the goal by setting $\alpha^G=(\alpha^L+\alpha^G)/2$).

Provide the precise control-flow summarized in the paper's pseudocode (Algorithm 1): initialize WCP empty and $\alpha^G=\alpha^L$ (the best manual baseline); loop indefinitely: run Adam SGD for 500 epochs on batches composed as described, if average loss over these epochs exceeds the adaptive threshold then continue training (skip MIPs); otherwise run two MIPs with $\alpha^G$ to compute $\epsilon_L,\epsilon_R,\vec{\theta}_L,\vec{\theta}_R$ and add the latter two to WCP; if $\epsilon_L+\epsilon_R\le 0.001$ then set $\alpha^L=\alpha^G$ and update $\alpha^G=(\alpha^U+\alpha^G)/2$, else set $\alpha^G=(\alpha^L+\alpha^G)/2$; repeat.

Describe how the MIP outputs are logged and used as stopping/advancement signals: the algorithm records and reports $\epsilon_L,\epsilon_R,\vec{\theta}_L,\vec{\theta}_R$ after every MIP call; the scalar $\epsilon_L+\epsilon_R$ is compared to the threshold $0.001$ and if below it the algorithm treats the current target $\alpha^G$ as achieved for the purposes of advancing the goalpost toward the theoretical upper bound, otherwise it reduces the immediate objective so training remains feasible.

Note implementation details and practicalities referenced by the paper that affect WCT performance: the one-binary-per-node-per-agent MIP encoding is computationally expensive so the heuristic to avoid frequent MIP calls is crucial; the adaptive loss threshold's schedule and the specific random-sampling distribution used for random profiles are described in the appendix (these implementation choices directly influence when MIPs are invoked and therefore the tradeoff between SGD progress and certification rounds).

Start from the upstream primitive: the Worst-Case Training algorithm (WCT) with MIP certification (established in Conclusion 3) is available to evaluate subnetworks and to provide worst-case profiles; use WCT as the evaluation-and-scratch procedure for drawn tickets.

State the initial large-network setup and the goal: begin from a large RELU MLP (the experiments use architecture [20,20], i.e., two hidden layers with 20 nodes each) and aim to find a tiny trainable subnetwork (a "ticket") of a specified target size (e.g., 10 or 20 nodes) that is amenable to MIP-based certification because small subnetworks keep the number of MIP binary variables manageable.

Explain the node importance metric and pruning decision rule used to draw a ticket: for a node whose outgoing weights toward the next layer are $w_1,w_2,\dots,w_k$, define its importance as $\sum_i |w_i|$ and define its relative importance as this importance divided by the total importance of all nodes in the same layer; to prune one node, remove the globally least-relative-important node (the node with smallest relative importance among all nodes in the network).

Describe the iterative draw procedure to create a ticket: train the large network on random type profiles (and stored worst-case profiles from prior draws, if any) until the average loss falls below a threshold, then prune one node (the least relative importance) and repeat pruning steps until the subnetwork reaches the target ticket size; this produces a candidate tiny subnetwork (one draw).

"Scratch" the drawn ticket by running WCT on the drawn subnetwork: with the subnetwork's connectivity fixed, run the worst-case training algorithm (WCT) for a fixed computational budget (the experiments use 100 MIP rounds per ticket) to train the subnetwork and to obtain certified worst-case performance; this determines whether the drawn ticket is a viable, high-quality mechanism.

If the drawn ticket fails to achieve satisfactory certified performance, record its discovered worst-case profiles and incorporate them into subsequent draws to avoid re-drawing the same poor ticket: specifically, save the latest 16 worst-case profiles found during that ticket's WCT run and include them in the training data when drawing the next ticket; restoring the large network's parameters to the original initialization before each new draw preserves the same initial "ticket pot" so prior draw information (saved worst cases) excludes previously seen bad tickets.

Repeat the draw-and-scratch process multiple times to discover multiple distinct tickets: because the large network contains an exponential number of possible subnetworks by node-pruning, repeating draws (by pruning under the influence of different sampled training data including stored worst cases) yields a sequence of distinct candidate tickets from which the best performing ones can be selected.

Explain the ensemble construction that leverages multiple good tickets: combine the two best tickets (found from repeated draws) into a randomized ensemble mechanism by selecting between the two subnetworks with probability 0.5 each; this ensemble is implemented as a MLP with an additional linear layer and its worst-case performance is analyzed and certified using the same MIP procedures; empirically this ensemble often improves certified worst-case performance because distinct tickets tend to have different worst-case profiles that "cover for each other".

Summarize the empirical ablation comparisons showing superiority to reinitialization baselines: the paper compares the lottery-pruning pipeline (Lott.) against three reinitialization baselines — Reinit1 (directly initialize small networks each draw), Reinit2 (like Reinit1 but do not share worst-case profiles across draws), and Reinit0 (reuse the same initialization across draws) — and reports across multiple experiments that the lottery-drawing procedure substantially outperforms these baselines in terms of achieved minimal gaps to theoretical upper bounds (see Table 2), demonstrating the practical benefit of pruning-from-large and sharing worst-case profiles between draws.

Conclude that the combination of the lottery-ticket pipeline, worst-case training (WCT), and exact MIP certification produces mechanisms that substantially improve the best previously-known manual worst-case gaps for a range of $n$, and that randomized ensembles of top tickets provide additional certified improvement in worst-case performance.

State the empirical concern: Monte Carlo sampling-based worst-case estimation evaluates a mechanism by checking its performance on randomly sampled type profiles rather than seeking exact worst-case maximizers; this can fail to find rare adversarial profiles leading to much larger constraint violations than seen in a finite random sample.

Present the explicit empirical example given in the paper that quantifies the phenomenon: the paper reports a mechanism found for $n=10$ whose exact worst-case allocative efficiency ratio, as computed by the MIP certification procedure, is $0.685$, whereas Monte Carlo evaluation over $10{,}000$ random type profiles reports an inflated ratio of $0.765$, i.e., Monte Carlo overestimates performance by about $0.080$ in this example.

Conclude the methodological implication: the demonstrated magnitude of Monte Carlo optimism motivates the use of exact worst-case MIP certification during both training (to discover true worst-case profiles as hard negatives) and final evaluation (to obtain certified worst-case guarantees), because Monte Carlo can be overly optimistic and may hide significant violations.

open_questions.content: The paper documents several unresolved scientific and practical issues. First, the lottery-ticket pruning procedure is empirical: there is no theoretical guarantee that repeated draws from a fixed initial large network will find a "winning" tiny trainable subnetwork within any computable number of draws; proving conditions under which such a winning ticket must exist (or bounding the draws needed) remains open. Second, the MIP-based exact certification scales poorly because it needs one binary per network node per agent; the approach reaches practical scalability limits around $n\approx 20$ with very small tickets (e.g., 6 nodes) and 128 GB memory; developing certified worst-case search methods that scale to larger $n$ or to larger subnetworks (for example via tighter continuous relaxations, symmetry exploitation, or alternative exact-certification encodings) is left open. Third, while the paper identifies (near-)optimal mechanisms for $n\in\{3,4,5\}$, for $n\ge 6$ the true optimal worst-case mechanisms remain unknown and whether the theoretical upper bounds are tight for all $n\ge 6$ is unresolved. Fourth, all discovered near-optimal mechanisms are obtained via floating-point-trained RELU networks: floating-point numerical error prevents formal exact-symbolic proofs of optimality, so producing exact rational or symbolic descriptions of the optimal $h$ functions (and proving optimality analytically) is an open task. Finally, the conjectured multiplicity and structural characterization of optimal mechanisms for larger $n$ (the paper suspects many optimal mechanisms exist for $n\ge 4$) is not established; understanding the combinatorial or geometric structure of the set of optimal Groves terms remains an open theoretical question.
